title: RDT based upper bounds on the largest average submatrix values
abstract: We study statistical variants of the classical largest average submatrix problem. For small submatrices (where the dimension is less than linearly proportional to the original matrix), the problem is typically well understood and believed to exhibit the statistical-computational gap (SCG). However, analytical treatment of both the information-theoretic and algorithmic aspects of the linear regime remains challenging, and no mathematically rigorous results have yet arrived anywhere close to proving or disproving SCG existence in this setting.   Focusing on the linear regime, we make strong progress in several key directions: 1) We develop a generic Random Duality Theory (RDT) framework to characterize largest average submatrix values. 2) Using the plain RDT variant, we obtain closed-form upper bounds as explicit functions of dimensionality proportionality parameters. 3) We demonstrate that a lifted RDT variant strictly improves upon the plain RDT within a certain linear range of submatrix dimensions. 4) For small submatrices where the dimensional proportionality constants approach zero, we prove that our results match both the replica results from [34] (obtained via one-step replica symmetry breaking) and the sublinear results from [18,45].
summary: This paper tackles the challenging statistical problem of finding upper bounds for the largest average submatrix value in random matrices. The authors introduce a novel Random Duality Theory (RDT) framework to rigorously characterize these bounds. By developing plain and lifted RDT variants, they provide explicit, improved upper bounds that match established results in the limit of small submatrices.
main_problem: The paper studies statistical variants of the classical largest average submatrix problem (LASP) for random matrices.
main_result: The authors developed a Random Duality Theory (RDT) framework to derive explicit, closed-form upper bounds on the largest average submatrix values, showing improvements over previous bounds.
method: The primary method is the development and application of a generic Random Duality Theory (RDT) framework, comparing plain and lifted variants to establish rigorous upper bounds.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on an $m 	imes n$ matrix $A$ whose elements are independent standard normal random variables. The problem is analyzed in the linear regime where submatrix dimensions are proportional to the original matrix dimensions.
key_observables: The largest average submatrix value ($\xi$), scaled by $\sqrt{n}$, which is the primary quantity of interest.
important_parameters: Dimensionality proportionality parameters ($\alpha,  eta_1,  eta_2$) and the regime where these parameters approach zero (small submatrices).
main_assumptions: The elements of the matrix $A$ are assumed to be independent standard normal random variables, and the analysis focuses on the asymptotic linear regime.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares the theoretical predictions (RDT and Lifted RDT) against algorithmic predictions (LAS) for the largest average submatrix value across different dimensions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the LASP in the statistical regime, develops the generic RDT framework, applies plain RDT to obtain initial bounds, introduces and utilizes a lifted RDT variant for tighter bounds, and finally validates these results by showing agreement with known replica and sublinear results in the small submatrix limit.
why_interesting: While the core topic is random matrix theory, the mathematical techniques involving duality, bounding, and analyzing phase transitions in high-dimensional random structures are highly relevant to understanding complexity in quantum information and many-body systems.
